Before 1945 democracies were few, so the absence of war between them may partly be statistical rarity. Layne (1994) examined near-wars between democracies, including Fashoda, and argued they were resolved by power calculations rather than liberal norms. Rosato (2003) argued the causal logic fails because democracies have not reliably externalised norms. Others offer rival explanations: Gartzke's capitalist peace attributes peace to market development, and after 1945 most democracies were allied under US leadership against a common Soviet threat. Democracies' covert operations against elected governments, such as Iran in 1953 and Guatemala in 1954, also suggest liberal solidarity is conditional.

The regularity itself has survived these challenges well: no unambiguous war between mature democracies has emerged. But a law implies a known causal mechanism and deterministic application, and the democratic peace is probabilistic, sensitive to definitions and its cause remains contested. It is best described as a strong empirical regularity with several plausible, partly overlapping explanations rather than a law.

questions.q: In Wallerstein's world-systems theory, which zone both exploits the periphery and is exploited by the core?
options: The core
The semi-periphery
The periphery
The external arena
questions.why: The semi-periphery occupies an intermediate position and acts as a political buffer that stabilises the capitalist world-economy.

questions.q: Robert Cox (1981) distinguished problem-solving theory from critical theory. Which statement best captures his criticism of problem-solving theory?
options: Its empirical predictions have proved false
It takes the prevailing order as given and so helps it run smoothly, implicitly serving existing power relations
It ignores the role of individual leaders
It is too normative and insufficiently scientific
questions.why: Cox argued problem-solving theory treats existing institutions and power relations as fixed, whereas critical theory asks how orders arise and can be changed; hence theory is always for someone and some purpose.

questions.q: Explain how dependency theory accounts for underdevelopment in the Global South and give one criticism of it.
markScheme: Periphery incorporated into world capitalism on unequal terms, with surplus extracted to the core
Frank's 'development of underdevelopment': underdevelopment caused by integration, not its absence
Specialisation in primary commodities and declining terms of trade (Prebisch–Singer)
A valid criticism, e.g. East Asian export-led development (South Korea, Taiwan) or Cardoso's dependent development
questions.modelAnswer: Dependency theorists argue that underdevelopment is not an original condition but the result of how peripheral economies were incorporated into world capitalism. Colonial and post-colonial structures locked the South into exporting primary commodities and importing manufactures, while profits flowed to core-based firms; Frank called this the 'development of underdevelopment'. The Prebisch–Singer thesis added that commodity prices tend to fall relative to manufactures, so the periphery must export ever more to buy the same imports. Critics point to South Korea and Taiwan, which industrialised rapidly through export-oriented integration, suggesting dependence is not destiny.

questions.q: Costavera, a fictional lower-middle-income state, earns 70 per cent of its export revenue from two commodities, coffee and copper. Over the past twenty years its export volumes have risen by 30 per cent, but the price of its exports relative to the price of its imports (its net barter terms of trade) has fallen by 25 per cent. Most copper mines are foreign-owned and repatriate the bulk of their profits. After a debt crisis, Costavera accepted an IMF loan conditional on privatising the state electricity company and cutting tariffs on manufactured imports. (a) Calculate the change in Costavera's purchasing power of exports (income terms of trade) and explain its significance. (b) Analyse Costavera's position using dependency theory and world-systems theory. (c) Evaluate these Marxist-influenced accounts against a liberal explanation of Costavera's situation.
markScheme: Correct calculation: 1.30 × 0.75 = 0.975, a fall of 2.5 per cent in import purchasing power
Interprets: Costavera exports more yet can buy fewer imports; links to Prebisch–Singer
Dependency theory: specialisation in primary goods and surplus extraction via profit repatriation; Frank's development of underdevelopment
World-systems theory: peripheral position, unequal exchange with the core, role of core-based capital
Critical/Gramscian reading of IMF conditionality as reproducing a neoliberal (Washington Consensus) order
Liberal explanation: comparative advantage, domestic governance and policy failures, integration as route to growth
Counter-evidence: East Asian export-led industrialisation; commodity booms such as the 2000s that improved some exporters' terms of trade
Cardoso and Faletto's dependent development as a nuanced middle position
Compares policy implications (diversification, renegotiating mining contracts, industrial policy vs liberalisation)
Balanced, well-structured judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The income terms of trade multiply export volume by the net barter terms of trade: 1.30 × 0.75 = 0.975. Despite exporting 30 per cent more, Costavera can buy about 2.5 per cent fewer imports than twenty years ago. It is running harder to stand still, and the extra output, labour and resource depletion have produced no gain in import capacity.

(b) This is the pattern the Prebisch–Singer thesis predicted and that dependency theory explains structurally. Costavera's role in the international division of labour, inherited from its colonial past, is to supply primary goods whose prices tend to fall relative to manufactures. Foreign ownership of mines means much of the surplus leaves the country as repatriated profit, which Frank would describe as the development of underdevelopment: integration enriches the metropole at the satellite's expense. Wallerstein's world-systems theory locates Costavera in the periphery, linked to the core by unequal exchange. Gramscian scholars such as Cox would read IMF conditionality, with privatisation and tariff cuts, as part of a neoliberal hegemony in which core interests are presented as universal economic sense; the reforms make industrialisation through protection harder.

(c) A liberal account would stress comparative advantage: specialising in coffee and copper is efficient, and the problem lies in domestic governance, weak institutions, failure to save commodity revenues and insufficient diversification. Liberals would note that foreign investment brought capital and technology the state lacked, and that open trade lowers consumer prices. They point to South Korea and Taiwan, which escaped the periphery by integrating through exports, and to the 2000s commodity boom, when many exporters' terms of trade improved, as evidence that decline is not inevitable.

The Marxist accounts are strongest at explaining why Costavera's structural position constrains it and why the gains from trade are unevenly shared. They are weaker at explaining why some peripheral states have moved up, and they risk understating domestic agency. Cardoso and Faletto's idea of dependent development offers a middle path: Costavera could grow, but on terms set by foreign capital. A sensible conclusion is that structure and policy both matter; diversification, better mining contracts and selective industrial policy respond to the dependency diagnosis without abandoning trade.

questions.q: 'Marxism offers a critique of international relations, not a theory of it.' Discuss. In your answer, consider what distinguishes an explanatory theory from a critique, and assess the explanatory claims of at least three Marxist or Marxist-influenced approaches (for example Lenin's theory of imperialism, Wallerstein's world-systems theory, Cox's Gramscian analysis or Rosenberg's work on uneven and combined development), set against the criticisms made by mainstream IR theorists.
markScheme: Clarifies the distinction between explanatory theory (causal claims, expectations) and critique (exposing interests, emancipatory purpose)
Lenin's Imperialism as an explanatory theory of war among capitalist powers, with testable claims and a mixed record
Waltz's critique that Hobson–Lenin theories are reductionist
Wallerstein's world-systems theory as a systemic, structural theory with explanatory claims about core–periphery relations and hegemonic cycles
Cox's distinction between problem-solving and critical theory; Gramscian hegemony as an explanatory concept for world orders
Rosenberg's uneven and combined development as an attempt to theorise 'the international' itself
Strengths: puts capitalism, class and inequality at the centre; illuminates globalisation and North–South relations
Weaknesses: economic determinism, underplays nationalism and state autonomy, struggles with wars between socialist states (Sino-Soviet clashes 1969, Sino-Vietnamese war 1979)
Reflects that the theory/critique distinction is itself questioned by Cox's claim that all theory serves a purpose
Clear argument and justified conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
An explanatory theory makes causal claims and generates expectations about outcomes; a critique exposes the interests hidden in existing arrangements and theories, often with an emancipatory aim. Marxism plainly does the second. The question is whether it also does the first.

Lenin's Imperialism (1917) was unmistakably explanatory. Building on Hobson, it argued that monopoly and finance capital needed outlets for surplus capital, so the great powers divided the world and, as development was uneven, fought to redivide it in 1914. It produced a testable expectation: wars among capitalist powers are inevitable. The record since 1945, with no war among the core capitalist states, tells against it, and Waltz criticised the theory as reductionist, explaining systemic outcomes by the attributes of units and unable to account for conflict among non-capitalist states.

Wallerstein's world-systems theory is, if anything, more systemic than Lenin. It explains the persistence of global inequality through a single capitalist world-economy with core, semi-periphery and periphery, and offers expectations about hegemonic cycles and mobility within the hierarchy. Whatever its empirical weaknesses, it is a theory in the full sense.

Cox's Gramscian approach blends both functions. His critique of problem-solving theory is famous, but his concept of hegemony as a fit between material power, ideas and institutions explains how world orders such as the Pax Americana are formed and how they change. Rosenberg's revival of uneven and combined development goes further, claiming to explain why there is an international dimension at all: societies develop unevenly and interactively, generating multiplicity.

The weaknesses are real. Marxist approaches tend towards economic determinism, underplay nationalism and the autonomy of state security interests, and struggle with wars between socialist states such as the Sino-Soviet border clashes of 1969 and the Sino-Vietnamese war of 1979. But weakness is not absence: these are flawed theories, not mere critiques.

Finally, the dichotomy itself is questionable. Cox's point that theory is always for someone and for some purpose implies mainstream theories also carry normative commitments. Marxism is distinctive in making its critique explicit, not in lacking explanation. The proposition therefore understates Marxism: it offers both critique and theory, and its theoretical claims deserve to be assessed on their merits.

questions.q: In Finnemore and Sikkink's (1998) norm life cycle, what mainly drives the 'norm cascade' stage?
options: Norm entrepreneurs persuading a critical mass of states through organisational platforms
Socialisation, as states adopt the norm after a tipping point to gain legitimacy, esteem and conformity
Habit and institutionalisation, so the norm is taken for granted
Coercion by a hegemonic state
questions.why: The cascade follows a tipping point and is driven by socialisation and states' desire for legitimacy; persuasion by entrepreneurs marks emergence, and habit marks internalisation.

questions.q: What does Wendt mean by the claim that 'anarchy is what states make of it'?
markScheme: The absence of world government does not by itself determine self-help or power politics
What anarchy means depends on identities and interests formed through interaction, so it can be competitive or cooperative
questions.modelAnswer: Wendt (1992) argues that the absence of a world government does not by itself force states into self-help and power politics, as neorealists claim. What anarchy means depends on the identities and interests states develop through interaction: anarchy among enemies is competitive, but anarchy among friends can be cooperative.

questions.q: Using securitisation theory, explain how an issue such as migration can be 'securitised' and why this matters.
markScheme: A securitising actor uses a speech act to present the issue as an existential threat to a referent object
The relevant audience must accept the framing for securitisation to succeed
Successful securitisation legitimises extraordinary measures beyond normal politics
Significance: threats are constructed, not simply objective; securitisation can bypass democratic scrutiny, hence Wæver's preference for desecuritisation (with an example)
questions.modelAnswer: For the Copenhagen School (Buzan, Wæver and de Wilde, 1998), security is a speech act. A securitising actor, such as a government, presents migration as an existential threat to a referent object like national identity or sovereignty. If the relevant audience accepts this framing, the issue is lifted out of normal politics and extraordinary measures, such as border fences, mass detention or emergency powers, become legitimate. This matters because it shows threats are constructed rather than simply objective, and because securitisation can bypass democratic scrutiny; Wæver therefore generally favours desecuritisation. Hungary's 2015 border fence illustrates the process.

questions.q: The United Kingdom possesses more than 200 nuclear warheads, yet the United States does not regard them as a threat; North Korea has far fewer, yet Washington treats its arsenal as a grave danger. Meanwhile France and Germany, which fought three major wars between 1870 and 1945, now share a currency and an open border and regard war between them as unthinkable, even though both maintain substantial armed forces. (a) Explain how Wendt's constructivism accounts for these two puzzles, using his three cultures of anarchy. (b) Assess how structural realism would explain the same facts. (c) Evaluate which approach offers the more convincing account of the Franco-German case, considering how identities change and whether such change could be reversed.
markScheme: Wendt's claim that material capabilities acquire meaning through shared understandings; the British vs North Korean missiles example
US–UK relationship as Kantian friendship versus Hobbesian enmity with North Korea
Explains the three cultures (Hobbesian, Lockean, Kantian) and degrees of internalisation (force, price, legitimacy)
Franco-German transformation through interaction, institutions (ECSC 1951, Élysée Treaty 1963, EU) and shared democratic identity; Deutsch's security community
Realist account of US–UK vs North Korea: balance of threat, alliance and perceived intentions
Realist account of Franco-German peace: US hegemony and NATO, the Soviet threat, nuclear deterrence
Mearsheimer's 1990 'Back to the Future' prediction of post-Cold War instability in Europe and its poor record
Notes Walt's inclusion of intentions concedes ground to ideational factors
Considers reversibility: identities are sticky but can erode; nationalist or populist pressures
Coherent, well-justified conclusion using accurate evidence
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For Wendt, material capabilities do not speak for themselves. In his well-known example, 500 British nuclear weapons are less threatening to the US than 5 North Korean ones, because the meaning of weapons depends on the relationship in which they are embedded. The US and UK share a Kantian culture of anarchy: each sees the other as a friend, settles disputes without force and expects mutual help. The US and North Korea are locked in a Hobbesian culture of enmity, in which each assumes the other may use unlimited violence. The Franco-German case shows that cultures change. After three wars, the two states built dense institutions, from the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) and the Élysée Treaty (1963) to the EU and the euro, and came to share a democratic, European identity. Repeated cooperative interaction moved them from Hobbesian enmity through Lockean rivalry to a Kantian security community, in Deutsch's sense of dependable expectations of peaceful change. Once internalised as legitimate, peace is no longer a calculation but part of who they are.

(b) Structural realists would answer that what matters is threat, not identity. Walt's balance of threat already includes perceived intentions: Britain is an ally whose arsenal is integrated with NATO, whereas North Korea is hostile and close to US allies. Franco-German peace is explained by the bipolar Cold War structure: US hegemony and NATO pacified Western Europe, a common Soviet threat aligned their interests and nuclear deterrence made war too costly.

(c) The realist account struggles with what happened after 1991. Mearsheimer predicted in 1990 that the end of bipolarity would bring renewed instability to Europe, even mentioning German nuclear acquisition, but Franco-German relations remained close and integration deepened. Moreover, Walt's reliance on intentions concedes the constructivist point that ideas shape how power is read. Constructivism therefore offers the more convincing account of this case. Its weakness is predicting when and why identities change, and it must admit reversibility: Wendt himself allows that cultures can regress. Rising nationalism or the collapse of shared institutions could erode trust, but the depth of internalisation makes rapid reversal unlikely.

questions.q: 'Constructivism is not a theory of international politics but a social ontology: it tells us what to look at, not what to expect.' Critically evaluate this claim. You should consider constructivism's core commitments, whether particular constructivist research programmes generate testable expectations, and the criticisms made from realist, methodological and more radical (poststructuralist) perspectives.
markScheme: Distinguishes social ontology/metatheory from substantive theory; notes Wendt presents constructivism as a social theory on which a substantive theory can be built
Explains core commitments: mutual constitution of agents and structures, constitutive role of ideas, logic of appropriateness
Shows research programmes yielding expectations: Finnemore and Sikkink's norm life cycle (tipping point, cascade), Tannenwald's nuclear taboo, Katzenstein's Culture of National Security
Wendt's Social Theory as a systemic theory with expectations, e.g. the three cultures and possible progression toward Kantian culture
Realist critique: ideas epiphenomenal to power; intentions unknowable; Mearsheimer's 'False Promise' critique
Methodological critique: measuring norms and identities, risk of post hoc explanation, bias toward 'good' norms
Poststructuralist critique: Wendt's 'thin' constructivism too close to positivist mainstream
Constructivism's success in explaining change, e.g. the end of the Cold War, where neorealism struggled
Considers combinations such as realist constructivism (Barkin) showing constructivism needs substantive assumptions
Clear structure and justified judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition captures something constructivists themselves concede. Wendt presents constructivism as a social theory about how the international system is constituted, on which a substantive theory of international politics can then be built. Its core commitments are ontological: agents and structures are mutually constituted, ideas constitute interests and identities rather than merely influencing behaviour, and actors often follow a logic of appropriateness rather than consequences. On its own, the claim that the world is socially constructed predicts nothing in particular; a constructed world could be peaceful or violent.

Yet the proposition understates what constructivist research programmes deliver once they add substantive content. Finnemore and Sikkink's norm life cycle specifies stages, actors and mechanisms, and even a tipping point, which they suggest rarely comes before about a third of states have adopted a norm, after which adoption accelerates through socialisation. Tannenwald's nuclear taboo yields expectations about how leaders discuss and reject nuclear use, which she tests against archival evidence from Korea, Vietnam and the Gulf. Katzenstein's Culture of National Security explains why states with similar power positions, such as Germany and Japan, adopted distinctive security policies. Wendt's own Social Theory proposes three cultures of anarchy and suggests mechanisms that could push systems towards Kantian cooperation.

Criticisms remain. Realists argue ideas are epiphenomenal to power and that because intentions cannot be known with certainty, states must still plan for the worst; Mearsheimer's 'False Promise' critique made this point against critical theories. Methodologically, norms and identities are hard to measure independently of the behaviour they are meant to explain, inviting post hoc reasoning, and early work focused disproportionately on 'good' norms such as the landmine ban. From the other side, poststructuralists argue that Wendt's state-centric, scientific-realist version is so close to the mainstream that it loses critical force.

Constructivism's record in explaining change is a strong counter to the proposition. The peaceful end of the Cold War, driven partly by Gorbachev's new thinking, was something neorealism neither predicted nor easily explains. Barkin's 'realist constructivism' illustrates the underlying point: constructivism can be combined with different substantive assumptions about power and interest.

The claim is therefore half right. As a metatheory, constructivism tells us what to look at. But the programmes built on it do tell us what to expect, so it is better seen as a family of theories sharing a social ontology.

questions.q: Which scholar asked 'Where are the women?' in Bananas, Beaches and Bases (1989)?
options: J. Ann Tickner
Cynthia Enloe
Jean Bethke Elshtain
Carol Cohn
questions.why: Enloe used the question to reveal women's often invisible roles in international politics; Tickner, Elshtain and Cohn wrote other key feminist IR works.

questions.q: UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000) is best described as:
options: A treaty criminalising sexual violence in armed conflict

The first Security Council resolution linking women's experiences of conflict to international peace and security, calling for their participation in peace processes and protection from gender-based violence
The resolution establishing the International Criminal Court
A General Assembly declaration on gender equality in employment
questions.why: Resolution 1325 founded the Women, Peace and Security agenda; it is a Security Council resolution, not a treaty, and the ICC was created by the 1998 Rome Statute.

questions.q: How does Tickner (1988) reformulate Morgenthau's principles of political realism, in particular his claims about objectivity and about interest defined as power?
markScheme: Tickner accepts realism describes much state behaviour but argues its principles reflect a masculine worldview
Objectivity is culturally associated with masculinity; all knowledge is partial and situated
Power as domination and control is privileged; she adds power as collective empowerment/acting in concert
National interest is multidimensional and context-dependent; nuclear, economic and environmental problems require cooperative responses
Her aim is a more complete realism, not a wholesale rejection
questions.modelAnswer: Tickner (1988) accepts that Morgenthau captures much state behaviour but argues his principles reflect a masculine worldview. His 'objective laws' rest on a notion of objectivity culturally associated with masculinity; Tickner holds that all knowledge is partial and situated. Interest defined as power privileges power as domination and control and ignores power as collective empowerment, or acting in concert. She reformulates the national interest as multidimensional and context-dependent: global problems such as nuclear danger, economic well-being and environmental degradation need cooperative rather than zero-sum responses. Her aim is not to discard realism but to make it more complete by including excluded perspectives.

questions.q: 'Feminist International Relations merely adds women to existing analyses; it does not change how we understand international politics.' Discuss this claim with reference to the work of Tickner and Enloe and at least one other feminist scholar. Consider both the conceptual and empirical contributions of feminist IR, and whether critics are right that it lacks a distinctive research agenda.
markScheme: Explains the 'add women and stir' charge and the liberal feminist focus on inclusion and representation
Tickner's epistemological critique of Morgenthau: objectivity, power and national interest as gendered
Enloe's method of asking 'where are the women?' revealing the gendered labour sustaining IR
Gender as an analytical category (masculinities and femininities), not merely a variable
Cohn's analysis of strategic discourse showing how gendered language shapes what is thinkable
Empirical contributions: sexual violence in war, the WPS agenda, Hudson et al.
Engages critics, e.g. Keohane's call for testable hypotheses and Tickner's 1997 reply on methodological difference
Reasoned conclusion that feminism reconceptualises rather than merely adds
questions.modelAnswer:
The charge of 'add women and stir' fairly describes one strand of feminist work. Liberal feminists highlight women's under-representation in foreign ministries, militaries and peace negotiations and campaign for inclusion, as in UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000). Valuable as this is, it leaves the discipline's core concepts untouched.

Most feminist IR goes much further. Tickner's (1988) reformulation of Morgenthau argued that realism's supposedly neutral concepts are gendered: objectivity is associated with masculinity, power is defined as domination, and the national interest is narrowed to military security. Rethinking power as collective empowerment and security as multidimensional changes what counts as international politics, not merely who is studied.

Enloe's question, 'where are the women?', is a method rather than a headcount. In Bananas, Beaches and Bases she shows that diplomatic wives, plantation workers and women around military bases perform labour that makes alliances, trade and war possible. Her claim that the personal is international redraws the boundary between domestic and international, private and public.

Cohn's study of US defence intellectuals demonstrates that gendered, euphemistic language made nuclear war thinkable and marginalised concern for human suffering, showing how gender shapes strategic reasoning itself. These works treat gender as a structure of power involving masculinities as much as women.

Empirically, feminist scholarship drove recognition of sexual violence as a weapon of war, leading to the Akayesu judgment (1998) and UNSCR 1820 (2008), and Hudson and colleagues have linked the treatment of women to state peacefulness.

Critics such as Keohane urged feminists to produce testable hypotheses to join the mainstream. Tickner's 1997 reply argued that feminist questions about meaning and power require different methods, so the misunderstanding is epistemological. That some feminist work is additive does not make the field so.

The claim therefore fails. Feminist IR does add women, but its main contribution is to show that core concepts are gendered, which changes how international politics is understood.

questions.q: After an eight-year civil war in the fictional state of Kesaria, internationally mediated peace talks are under way. Of the 14 negotiators, one is a woman. The draft agreement contains a general amnesty for conflict-related crimes, including sexual violence, which the armed groups insist on as a condition of signing. The proposed disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration (DDR) programme offers cash and training only to those who hand in a weapon, although human rights monitors estimate that thousands of women and girls served the rebels as porters, cooks, fighters and forced 'wives'. Donors propose a 30 per cent quota for women in the transitional parliament. Using feminist IR theory and relevant international law and practice, critically evaluate the draft settlement and recommend changes. You should consider whether feminist priorities conflict with the goal of securing an agreement the armed groups will sign.
markScheme: Applies UNSCR 1325's participation and protection pillars to the composition of the negotiating team

Assesses the amnesty against developments in international law: Akayesu (1998), Kunarac (2001), the Rome Statute (1998) listing rape and sexual slavery as crimes, and UNSCR 1820 (2008) on excluding sexual violence from amnesty provisions
Critiques weapon-based DDR eligibility, citing Sierra Leone, where many women and girls associated with armed groups were excluded
Uses Enloe to reveal women's hidden roles in war economies and armed groups
Uses Sjoberg and Gentry or critiques of essentialism: women are combatants and agents, not only victims or natural peacemakers
Considers masculinities: male survivors of sexual violence; militarised masculinity in reintegration
Evaluates the quota from liberal feminist (inclusion) and critical feminist (tokenism, elite capture) perspectives
Draws on a real comparison, e.g. Colombia's 2016 agreement and its gender sub-commission
Weighs feminist recommendations against the peace-versus-justice dilemma and realist concerns about spoilers
Makes concrete, prioritised recommendations
Clear structure and coherent judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
Kesaria's draft reproduces the gender blindness feminist IR has long criticised. With one woman among 14 negotiators, it falls short of UNSCR 1325's call for women's participation in peace processes, and the consequences are visible in its content.

First, the blanket amnesty. Since the ICTR's Akayesu judgment (1998) recognised rape as an act of genocide, and the ICTY's Kunarac judgment (2001) treated rape and sexual enslavement as crimes against humanity, international law has moved firmly against impunity. The Rome Statute lists rape and sexual slavery as war crimes and crimes against humanity, and UNSCR 1820 (2008) stresses excluding sexual violence crimes from amnesty provisions. An amnesty covering such crimes would deny survivors justice and signal that bodies are legitimate bargaining chips.

Second, the DDR criterion. Enloe's question, 'where are the women?', exposes how defining a combatant by weapon handover erases women's roles as porters, cooks, fighters and forced 'wives'. Sierra Leone's DDR process had this effect, leaving many women and girls without support or recognition. Sjoberg and Gentry warn against treating women only as victims: some were fighters with agency, and all need reintegration. Feminists would also highlight masculinities: demobilised men stripped of militarised status may turn to domestic violence, and male survivors of sexual violence are often ignored.

Third, the quota. Liberal feminists would welcome 30 per cent representation, which Colombia's 2016 agreement, shaped by a gender sub-commission, suggests can embed gender provisions. Critical feminists caution that quotas can produce token or elite women while leaving gendered power untouched.

The hardest issue is the peace-versus-justice dilemma. Realist-minded mediators argue armed elites will not sign if they face prosecution, and a failed deal means continued violence, which also harms women. But feminist analysis questions whose peace is being bought.

I would recommend: enlarging the negotiating team and creating a gender sub-commission; replacing the blanket amnesty with conditional arrangements that exclude sexual violence, possibly with reduced sentences for truth-telling, as Colombia's transitional justice model attempted; redefining DDR eligibility by association with armed groups; and pairing the quota with funding for grassroots women's organisations. These changes raise the cost of agreement slightly but make the peace more legitimate and durable.

questions.q: In Fearon's (1995) bargaining model, a declining state's decision to fight now because a rising rival cannot credibly promise not to exploit its future strength is an example of:
options: Private information with incentives to misrepresent
A commitment problem
Issue indivisibility
Audience costs
questions.why: When power is shifting, the rising state cannot bind itself to honour today's bargain tomorrow, so preventive war becomes rational: a commitment problem.

questions.q: Distinguish pre-emptive war from preventive war, giving an example of each.
markScheme: Pre-emptive war: striking first against an attack believed to be imminent
Preventive war: fighting to forestall a future shift in the balance of power without an imminent threat
Appropriate examples, e.g. Israel June 1967 (pre-emptive); US-led invasion of Iraq 2003 or Israel's 1981 Osirak strike (preventive)
questions.modelAnswer: A pre-emptive war is launched to strike first against an attack believed to be imminent, as when Israel attacked Egypt in June 1967 amid Egyptian troop movements and the closure of the Straits of Tiran. A preventive war is fought to stop a long-term shift in the balance of power before a rival becomes stronger, even though no attack is imminent; the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, justified by possible future weapons of mass destruction, is a common example.

questions.q: Fearon argues that issue indivisibility is a less important cause of war than private information or commitment problems. Assess this claim.
markScheme: Explains indivisibility: a stake that cannot be divided, so no compromise within the bargaining range exists
Fearon's reasoning: most issues are divisible in principle via side payments, linkage, alternation or randomisation
Apparent indivisibility is often produced by domestic politics or leaders' framing
Powell (2006) recasts many indivisibility cases as commitment problems
Counter-argument: sacred or identity-laden stakes resist division, e.g. Hassner (2003) on sacred spaces, Toft (2003) on homeland territory
Reaches a judgement, e.g. persuasive within rationalist logic but underestimates ideational value
questions.modelAnswer: Fearon argues truly indivisible issues are rare: most stakes can in principle be divided through side payments, linkage to other issues, alternation or even chance, so indivisibility cannot by itself explain why bargains fail. Apparent indivisibility is often produced by domestic politics or leaders' framing. Powell (2006) goes further, recasting many indivisibility cases as commitment problems: a state refuses to concede part of a territory because doing so would shift future bargaining power against it. Critics reply that stakes with sacred or identity value resist compromise, citing Hassner (2003) on sacred spaces such as Jerusalem's holy sites and Toft (2003) on homeland territory. Fearon is persuasive within rationalist logic, but indivisibility matters more once ideational value is admitted.

questions.q: Two fictional states, Kordia and Lusan, dispute a border province worth 100 units to each. Both governments agree that if war broke out Kordia would win with probability 0.6. War would cost Kordia 10 units and Lusan 15 units. (a) Calculate each state's expected utility from war and identify the range of peaceful divisions of the province (expressed as Kordia's share) that both should prefer to war. (b) Now suppose Lusan privately comes to believe that its own chance of victory is 0.55, while Kordia still believes it will win with probability 0.6. Recalculate the range using each side's beliefs. Does a mutually acceptable deal still exist? What happens if Lusan's belief rises to 0.7? (c) Using Fearon (1995), explain why states cannot simply reveal their true strength to avoid war, and identify a real case where private information or a commitment problem plausibly contributed to war. (d) Evaluate the strengths and limitations of the rationalist bargaining approach.
markScheme: Expected utility of war: Kordia 0.6 × 100 − 10 = 50; Lusan 0.4 × 100 − 15 = 25
Bargaining range: Kordia's share between 50 and 75; width equals the combined costs of war (25)
Explains Fearon's puzzle: every deal in the range is better for both than war
At 0.55, Lusan requires at least 40, so Kordia's share must be at most 60; range 50–60 still exists
At 0.7, Lusan requires at least 55, so Kordia's share must be at most 45, below Kordia's minimum of 50: no deal; mutual optimism leads to war (cf. Blainey)
Explains incentives to misrepresent: bluffing for better terms makes claims of strength non-credible; revealing capabilities can reduce their military value
Explains the commitment problem with a real case, e.g. German fears of rising Russian power before 1914
Gives an information-failure case, e.g. Russia's underestimation of Ukrainian resistance in 2022
Evaluates strengths: parsimony, war as bargaining failure, fighting as information revelation
Evaluates limits: unitary rational actor assumption, domestic politics, ideology, emotion, leaders' private interests
Clear, accurate presentation of calculations and structured argument
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Kordia's expected utility from war is 0.6 × 100 − 10 = 50; Lusan's is 0.4 × 100 − 15 = 25. Kordia will accept any share of at least 50; Lusan will accept any deal leaving it at least 25, so Kordia's share can be at most 75. Any division giving Kordia between 50 and 75 is better for both than fighting. The range is 25 units wide, exactly the sum of the two sides' costs. This is Fearon's puzzle: because war destroys value, a peaceful bargain always exists if both sides agree on the odds.

(b) If Lusan believes it wins with probability 0.55, its expected war payoff is 55 − 15 = 40, so it now demands at least 40 and Kordia's share must be at most 60. Kordia still needs 50. A narrower range of 50 to 60 survives, so a deal is possible though harder to find. If Lusan's belief rises to 0.7, its war payoff becomes 70 − 15 = 55, so Kordia's share must be at most 45, below the 50 Kordia requires. No division satisfies both: mutual optimism about victory, which Blainey identified, eliminates the bargaining range and war becomes likely.

(c) Why not simply reveal the truth? Fearon's answer is that states have incentives to misrepresent: each gains better terms by appearing stronger or more resolved, so cheap claims are not credible. Revealing true capabilities, such as plans or force deployments, may also reduce their military value. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine illustrates information failure: Moscow appears to have badly underestimated Ukrainian resistance and Western support. Commitment problems arise when power is shifting; German leaders' fear before 1914 that Russia's military modernisation would soon tip the balance is often analysed as a preventive logic of this kind.

(d) The approach is powerful because it is parsimonious, reframes war as a bargaining failure, and explains why fighting often ends once battles reveal true strength. Its limits are its assumptions: states as unitary rational actors with shared values over the stake. It neglects domestic politics, leaders who gamble for personal survival, ideology, emotion and the possibility that the stake itself has non-material value. It identifies necessary conditions for war but needs other theories to explain when misperception or shifting power arise.

questions.q: 'Interstate war is in terminal decline.' Assess this claim in light of the evidence since 1945, including Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Your answer should distinguish between the frequency, severity and underlying propensity for war, evaluate the main explanations offered for any decline, and consider whether conflict has been displaced into other forms rather than disappearing.
markScheme: Defines interstate war (e.g. COW 1,000 battle-deaths threshold) and distinguishes frequency, severity and propensity
Presents the decline thesis: Mueller (obsolescence of major war), Pinker; fall in great-power war and conquest after 1945
Explanations: nuclear deterrence; democratic peace and interdependence; territorial integrity norm (Zacher 2001) and decline of state death (Fazal 2007); UN Charter Article 2(4)
Counter-evidence: Braumoeller (2019) that the propensity for war has not clearly declined; statistical problems with rare, heavy-tailed events
Post-1945 interstate wars: Korea, Iran–Iraq 1980–88, Eritrea–Ethiopia 1998–2000, Iraq 2003, Russia–Georgia 2008
Russia–Ukraine 2022 as the largest interstate war in Europe since 1945 and a direct challenge to the conquest norm
Other recent cases, e.g. Armenia–Azerbaijan 2020, India–Pakistan clashes 2025, as evidence of persistent risk
Substitution: civil wars, proxy wars, internationalised civil wars and grey-zone conflict
Theoretical evaluation: realist versus liberal and constructivist interpretations
Clear, justified conclusion on the word 'terminal'
questions.modelAnswer:
Whether interstate war is declining depends on what is measured. The frequency of wars between states (conventionally, sustained combat causing at least 1,000 battle deaths), their severity and the underlying propensity of states to fight are different things, and the evidence differs across them.

The decline thesis is strongest on frequency and on great-power war. Since 1945 the major powers have not fought each other directly, and outright conquest of states has become rare. Mueller argued major war had become obsolete, like duelling, and Pinker presented long-run declines in violence. Explanations multiply: nuclear deterrence raised the costs of great-power war; the democratic peace and economic interdependence reduced incentives among liberal states; Zacher (2001) documented a strengthening territorial integrity norm, and Fazal (2007) showed the near-disappearance of violent state death after 1945; the UN Charter's Article 2(4) delegitimised aggression.

But 'terminal' is too strong. Braumoeller (2019) argues the underlying propensity for war has not clearly fallen; because wars are rare events with heavy-tailed severity, a few decades of relative calm are statistically weak evidence. Serious interstate wars continued: Korea, Iran–Iraq (1980–88), Eritrea–Ethiopia (1998–2000), the 2003 Iraq war and Russia–Georgia (2008). Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 is the largest interstate war in Europe since 1945 and, with its formal annexation of Ukrainian territory, a direct challenge to the conquest norm. Armenia–Azerbaijan in 2020 and the India–Pakistan clashes of 2025 show that wars between states, including nuclear-armed ones, remain possible.

Conflict has also been displaced. Most post-1945 armed conflict has been civil, and many civil wars are internationalised by foreign intervention, as in Syria and Yemen. Proxy war, cyber operations and grey-zone coercion let states compete below the threshold of open war.

Theory shapes interpretation. Realists see the long peace as a product of bipolarity and nuclear weapons, contingent on structure that can change. Liberals and constructivists see institutional and normative change that is more durable but reversible if norms erode.

Overall, there has been a real decline in the frequency of interstate war and in conquest, but not convincing evidence that the propensity for war has disappeared. The decline is significant and conditional, not terminal.

questions.q: Fearon and Laitin (2003) found that the strongest predictors of civil war onset were conditions favouring insurgency. Which set of factors did they highlight?
options: High ethnic fractionalisation and religious diversity
Low per capita income, large population and mountainous terrain
Democratic government and free elections
High levels of income inequality
questions.why: Fearon and Laitin found poverty (weak state capacity), population and rough terrain mattered, while ethnic diversity was not significant once income was controlled.

questions.q: Which finding is associated with Fortna's Does Peacekeeping Work? (2008)?
options: Peacekeepers are sent only to easy cases, so they have no independent effect
Peacekeeping substantially reduces the risk of renewed war, even though peacekeepers tend to be sent to the more difficult cases
Partition is more effective than peacekeeping in preventing recurrence
Peacekeeping increases the risk of war by freezing conflicts
questions.why: Fortna controlled for the selection of hard cases and found that peacekeeping significantly lowers the hazard of war resuming.

questions.q: Contrast 'greed' and 'grievance' explanations of civil war and explain why Collier and Hoeffler's findings were controversial.
markScheme: Greed/opportunity: lootable resources, diaspora funding, low incomes making recruitment cheap
Grievance: inequality, political exclusion, repression, ethnic or religious hatred
Collier and Hoeffler found opportunity proxies predicted onset better than grievance measures
Controversy: ambiguous proxies (e.g. commodity dependence may indicate weak state capacity, Fearon 2005), delegitimising rebels' aims, later revival of grievance through ethnic exclusion research
questions.modelAnswer: Greed or opportunity explanations hold that rebellion occurs where it is profitable or feasible: lootable commodities, diaspora funding and low incomes that make recruitment cheap. Grievance explanations stress inequality, political exclusion, repression and ethnic or religious hatred. Collier and Hoeffler (2004) found opportunity proxies predicted civil war onset better than grievance measures. This was controversial because their proxies are ambiguous: primary commodity dependence may signal a weak, rentier state rather than looting opportunities (Fearon 2005). Critics also argued the framing delegitimised rebels' political aims, and later work on ethnic exclusion revived grievance-based explanations.

questions.q: A development agency asks you to assess the risk of civil war in two fictional countries. Ardania: GDP per capita $700; population 48 million; about 40 per cent of its territory is mountainous; oil accounts for 30 per cent of GDP; ethnic fractionalisation index 0.35; independent for only six years; a semi-democratic regime that has experienced two irregular changes of leader. Belvale: GDP per capita $9,500; population 12 million; mostly flat; diversified economy; ethnic fractionalisation index 0.80; stable electoral democracy; but one ethnic group comprising 30 per cent of the population has been excluded from cabinet posts and senior army ranks for two decades. (a) Using Fearon and Laitin (2003) and Collier and Hoeffler (2004), rank the two countries by risk of civil war onset, explaining which variables drive your judgement. (b) Show how research on ethnic exclusion and horizontal inequality (e.g. Cederman, Wimmer and Min 2010) might qualify your ranking. (c) Evaluate the limitations of cross-national statistical models for this kind of risk assessment.
markScheme: Fearon and Laitin: Ardania higher risk owing to low income (weak state capacity), large population, rough terrain, new statehood, political instability and oil
Collier and Hoeffler: Ardania higher risk owing to resource rents and low income lowering the opportunity cost of rebellion
Notes that Belvale's high fractionalisation does not raise risk in Fearon and Laitin, and Collier and Hoeffler found highly diverse societies may be safer than those with one dominant group
Belvale's income and stable democracy reduce risk in both models
Cederman, Wimmer and Min: exclusion from state power raises rebellion risk, especially for large groups; Belvale's excluded 30 per cent is a sizeable, mobilisable group
Horizontal inequality (Stewart; Cederman, Gleditsch and Buhaug 2013) restores grievance as a driver
Revised judgement: Ardania still higher overall, but Belvale's risk is not negligible and needs monitoring
Limitations: ambiguous proxies, endogeneity, rare events, poor out-of-sample prediction (Ward, Greenhill and Bakke 2010), ecological inference
Uses real cases, e.g. oil and the Niger Delta; exclusion of Sunni Arabs in post-2003 Iraq
Structured, policy-relevant judgement
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Both leading models place Ardania at much higher risk. For Fearon and Laitin, civil war is best explained by conditions that make insurgency feasible. Ardania's low income signals weak state capacity to police its territory, its large population makes control harder, its mountains offer rebels sanctuary, and it is a new state with recent political instability. Oil, which accounts for a large share of the economy, adds to risk by creating a lucrative prize and a state that relies on rents rather than building administrative reach. Collier and Hoeffler reach the same conclusion through opportunity: low incomes make recruitment cheap and natural resource rents can finance rebellion, with risk highest at intermediate-to-high levels of commodity dependence. Belvale looks safe on these measures: high income, a strong state, flat terrain and a diversified economy. Its high ethnic fractionalisation is not a risk factor for Fearon and Laitin once income is controlled, and Collier and Hoeffler found very diverse societies may be safer than those where one group dominates, because rebel coordination is harder.

(b) Research on ethnic exclusion complicates this. Cederman, Wimmer and Min (2010) found that groups excluded from state power are significantly more likely to rebel, especially when they are large. Belvale's excluded group comprises 30 per cent of the population and has been shut out of cabinet and senior army posts for two decades, a classic configuration of horizontal inequality. Later work by Cederman, Gleditsch and Buhaug (2013) linked such group-level inequalities to conflict, restoring grievance to the picture. Post-2003 Iraq, where the marginalisation of Sunni Arabs fuelled insurgency, is a cautionary case. Ardania remains higher risk overall, but Belvale's risk is not negligible and could rise if exclusion hardens or the democratic system is seen as closed.

(c) The models themselves have limits. Their proxies are ambiguous: low income can mean weak state capacity or low opportunity costs, and the two models interpret the same variable differently. Civil war is a rare event, so estimates are fragile, and causation can run both ways, since instability lowers income. Ward, Greenhill and Bakke (2010) showed that variables significant in such models often predict poorly out of sample. Cross-national averages also obscure local dynamics. They are a useful starting point, but the agency should combine them with qualitative country expertise and monitoring of political exclusion.

questions.q: 'Negotiated settlements of civil wars are inherently fragile; outright military victory produces a more durable peace.' Discuss this claim. In your answer, assess the main evidence on how civil wars end, the reasons settlements break down, the measures that can make them stick, and the moral and political costs of victory, using at least two real cases.
markScheme: Sets out Licklider (1995): negotiated settlements of identity wars more likely to break down than military victories; Toft (2010) on the stability of rebel victories
Explains why settlements fail: commitment problems during demobilisation (Walter); both sides retain fighting capacity
Counter-evidence: Walter on third-party guarantees; Fortna on peacekeeping; Hartzell and Hoddie on multidimensional power-sharing
Cases of relatively durable settlements, e.g. Mozambique 1992, Northern Ireland 1998, Colombia 2016 (with implementation problems)
Case of victory, e.g. Sri Lanka 2009: durable absence of war but heavy civilian toll and unresolved grievances
Normative costs of victory: atrocities, repression, exclusion; risk of renewed grievance
Selection effects: settlements tend to occur in harder, stalemated wars
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Early quantitative work supported the claim. Licklider (1995) found that identity civil wars ended by negotiated settlement were more likely to resume than those ended by military victory, and Toft (2010) argued that victories, especially rebel victories, produce the most durable peace because the loser's capacity to fight is destroyed.

The logic is a commitment problem. Walter (1997) showed that settlements require rebels to disarm, leaving them vulnerable to a government that cannot credibly promise not to exploit their weakness. Because both sides retain fighting capacity after a settlement, each fears the other will renege. Angola illustrates this: the 1991 Bicesse Accords collapsed after the disputed 1992 election.

But fragility is not inherent. Walter found that third-party security guarantees dramatically increase the chance that settlements are implemented. Fortna (2008) showed peacekeeping significantly reduces relapse, and Hartzell and Hoddie (2003) found that settlements sharing power across political, military, territorial and economic dimensions are more durable. Mozambique's 1992 accord, backed by a substantial UN mission, ended a brutal war, although low-level RENAMO violence resurfaced between 2013 and 2019. Northern Ireland's 1998 Good Friday Agreement used consociational power-sharing to end the Troubles. Colombia's 2016 agreement demobilised most of the FARC, despite serious implementation gaps and dissident groups.

There is also a selection effect: wars end in settlement when neither side can win, so negotiated outcomes are drawn disproportionately from the hardest cases. Comparing them with victories understates what settlements achieve.

Victory carries its own costs. Sri Lanka's defeat of the LTTE in 2009 ended the war, but the final offensive killed large numbers of civilians, and Tamil grievances over accountability and political representation remain unresolved. Victory can produce stability through repression and exclusion, which may simply defer conflict.

The claim therefore oversimplifies. Settlements are riskier in the short term, but their fragility stems from solvable commitment problems. With guarantees, peacekeeping and power-sharing they can be durable, and they avoid the moral and political costs that victory often entails.

questions.q: Under Article IX of the NPT, a 'nuclear-weapon state' is defined as one that:
options: Had manufactured and exploded a nuclear device before 1 January 1967
Is a permanent member of the UN Security Council
Possesses a secure second-strike capability
Declared its arsenal to the IAEA by 1970
questions.why: The treaty uses the 1 January 1967 test date; the five states it covers happen to be the permanent members of the Security Council, but that is not the legal criterion.

questions.q: What is a second-strike capability and why is it central to nuclear deterrence?
markScheme: The ability to absorb a first strike and still retaliate with unacceptable damage (e.g. via submarines, hardened or mobile launchers)
It removes the incentive to strike first, creating mutual vulnerability (MAD) and stable deterrence
questions.modelAnswer: A second-strike capability is the ability to absorb an enemy's nuclear first strike and still retaliate with unacceptable damage, usually through hardened silos, mobile launchers or submarines. It is central because if both sides possess one, neither gains anything by striking first, producing mutually assured destruction and stable deterrence.

questions.q: Outline Sagan's three models of why states build nuclear weapons and apply one of them to a real case.
markScheme: Security model: states build weapons to counter external threats, especially a nuclear-armed rival
Domestic politics model: weapons serve the interests of coalitions such as nuclear scientists, the military and politicians
Norms model: weapons as symbols of modernity, status and identity
Accurate application to a case, e.g. India 1974, France under de Gaulle, or South Africa's reversal
Evaluation: models are not mutually exclusive or note the limits of the chosen model
questions.modelAnswer: Sagan (1996) proposes three models. In the security model, states build bombs to counter external threats, especially a nuclear-armed rival. In the domestic politics model, weapons serve the interests of coalitions such as nuclear scientists, the military and politicians seeking popularity. In the norms model, weapons are symbols of modernity and status. Sagan applies the domestic model to India's 1974 test: China had tested in 1964, yet India waited a decade, and the timing reflected lobbying by the atomic energy establishment and Indira Gandhi's domestic political needs. The models are not mutually exclusive; security concerns clearly shaped India's long-term interest in a deterrent.

questions.q: Veloria, a fictional middle power and member of the NPT, borders a nuclear-armed rival with larger conventional forces that recently seized disputed islands in a short clash. Veloria already operates civilian enrichment facilities under IAEA safeguards. Its populist president, elected on a promise to 'restore national greatness', says Veloria 'deserves a seat at the top table'. The national atomic energy commission and parts of the military lobby for a weapons programme, while the finance ministry warns that sanctions could cut exports by a fifth. Veloria's great-power ally offers to deploy missile defences and to reaffirm an extended deterrence guarantee. (a) Apply Sagan's three models to explain the pressures towards proliferation. (b) Using the Waltz–Sagan debate, assess the likely consequences for regional stability if Veloria acquires nuclear weapons. (c) Recommend and justify the policy mix the ally should adopt to dissuade Veloria, drawing on real cases.
markScheme: Security model: nuclear-armed rival, conventional inferiority and territorial loss; weighs the credibility of the ally's guarantee
Domestic politics model: atomic energy commission and military as bureaucratic advocates; populist leader seeking legitimacy (cf. India 1974 and 1998)
Norms/prestige model: 'top table' rhetoric and nuclear weapons as status symbols (cf. France under de Gaulle); countervailing NPT norm
Credits Hymans' 'oppositional nationalist' leaders as a relevant psychological factor
Waltz: deterrence would stabilise the dyad and induce caution
Sagan: organisational risks: preventive war incentives during the transition, vulnerable early arsenals, accidents and unauthorised use, heightened by the recent clash
Stability–instability paradox: more low-level conflict over the islands (Kargil analogy)
Wider effects: regional cascade and erosion of the NPT (Article X withdrawal)

Policy mix: credible extended deterrence and reassurance (e.g. South Korea in the 1970s, West Germany), negotiated limits and inspections (JCPOA model), conditional economic incentives and sanctions, alternative sources of status
Considers risks: abandonment fears, coercion backfiring (North Korea), lessons drawn from Libya and Ukraine
Coherent, justified recommendation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Sagan's security model points to powerful external pressures. Veloria faces a nuclear-armed rival with conventional superiority that has just seized territory, so a bomb looks like the ultimate equaliser. Yet the security case depends on the credibility of the ally's guarantee: if extended deterrence is believed, the need for an independent arsenal falls. The domestic politics model is also strongly engaged. The atomic energy commission and parts of the military are classic bureaucratic advocates whose budgets and prestige would grow, and a populist president may see a bomb as a source of domestic legitimacy, much as Sagan argued for India in 1974. The norms model captures the 'top table' rhetoric: weapons as a symbol of great-power status, recalling de Gaulle's France. Hymans' work on 'oppositional nationalist' leaders suggests the president's worldview may matter as much as the threat. Countervailing norms, including NPT membership and the economic cost flagged by the finance ministry, pull the other way.

(b) Waltz would argue a Velorian bomb could stabilise the dyad: both sides would face unacceptable costs from major war and behave more cautiously, as new nuclear states historically have. Sagan's organisational critique is more worrying here. During the transition the rival might be tempted towards preventive strikes; an early Velorian arsenal may be vulnerable, encouraging use-it-or-lose-it thinking; and the recent clash means forces are on edge, raising accident risks. The stability–instability paradox suggests that even if major war is deterred, low-level fighting over the islands could increase, as at Kargil in 1999. It might also trigger a regional cascade, and Veloria would have to leave the NPT under Article X.

(c) The ally should combine reassurance with conditional incentives. Credible extended deterrence, including missile defences, consultations and visible commitments, addresses the security driver; US guarantees and pressure persuaded South Korea to halt its secret programme in the 1970s, and NATO arrangements helped keep West Germany non-nuclear. A negotiated framework limiting enrichment levels and expanding inspections, modelled on the JCPOA, would lengthen breakout time. Economic incentives tied to compliance, with sanctions held in reserve, address the finance ministry's concerns. Finally, offering status through regional leadership roles responds to the prestige motive. The ally must avoid coercion that confirms Velorian fears, recalling how North Korea responded to pressure, and must recognise that Libya's fate after disarming and Russia's violation of the Budapest assurances to Ukraine make guarantees harder to believe.

questions.q: 'More may be better.' Evaluate Kenneth Waltz's argument that the gradual spread of nuclear weapons promotes international stability, in light of Scott Sagan's critique and the historical record since 1945. You should consider both theoretical logic and evidence from specific nuclear dyads and crises, and assess what kinds of evidence could settle the debate.
markScheme: Waltz's argument: nuclear weapons make war's costs unbearable and outcomes uncertain; deterrence is easy; new nuclear states act cautiously; spread should be gradual
Waltz's evidence: no full-scale war between nuclear-armed states; socialisation of revolutionary states such as China after 1964
Sagan's organisational theory: military biases toward preventive war, failure to build survivable forces, accidents; weak civilian control in new nuclear states
Evidence from the Cuban Missile Crisis and near-accidents documented in The Limits of Safety (1993)
South Asia: Kargil 1999, the 2001–02 standoff, Balakot 2019, 2025 clashes; limited conflict without full war
North Korea: nuclear cover for provocations such as the 2010 Cheonan sinking and Yeonpyeong shelling
Non-state actors and leakage, e.g. the A. Q. Khan network
Waltz's 2012 argument that Iran should get the bomb and responses
Methodological point: small-n, absence of nuclear war may reflect luck; survivorship bias
Clear structure and nuanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Waltz's case is elegant. Nuclear weapons make the costs of war so catastrophic and the outcome so uncertain that even reckless leaders become cautious; deterrence requires only a survivable second-strike force, which is not hard to build. New nuclear states, he argued, are socialised by possession: China, feared as a revolutionary power in 1964, behaved conservatively as a nuclear state. Because no two nuclear-armed states have fought a full-scale war, gradual spread should extend this stability. In 2012 he even suggested an Iranian bomb could stabilise the Middle East by balancing Israel.

Sagan's critique attacks the assumption that states behave as unitary rational actors. Nuclear weapons are controlled by military organisations with predictable biases: they favour preventive war, may fail to build survivable forces during vulnerable transitions, and run complex systems in which accidents are 'normal'. In many new nuclear states civilian control is weak. Sagan's The Limits of Safety documented alarming near-accidents during the Cuban Missile Crisis, suggesting that even the most professional arsenals came close to catastrophe through error rather than design.

The record since 1945 offers support to both. South Asia is the key test. India and Pakistan have not fought a full-scale war since 1998, which Waltzians cite. But Pakistan's incursion at Kargil in 1999, the 2001–02 mobilisation, the Balakot strikes of 2019 and the clashes of 2025 show the stability–instability paradox at work: nuclear cover encourages limited aggression that could escalate. North Korea used its arsenal to shield provocations such as the sinking of the Cheonan and the shelling of Yeonpyeong in 2010. The A. Q. Khan network showed that spread can leak beyond states.

The evidence cannot settle the debate decisively. Nuclear war is a single catastrophic event; eighty years without one is consistent both with robust deterrence and with good luck, and we observe only the histories in which disaster was avoided. Sagan's point is that the cost of being wrong is asymmetric: deterrence must work every time.

On balance Waltz is persuasive that nuclear weapons discourage large deliberate wars between states. But his optimism underestimates organisational fallibility, limited war under the nuclear shadow and leakage risks. More may be safer in one narrow sense while making the world more dangerous overall.

questions.q: Which author is most associated with the 'hyperglobalist' claim that the nation-state is being made obsolete by a borderless world economy?
options: Kenichi Ohmae
Paul Hirst
Dani Rodrik
John Ruggie
questions.why: Ohmae's The Borderless World (1990) and The End of the Nation State (1995) are classic hyperglobalist texts; Hirst (with Thompson) is a sceptic.

questions.q: According to Rodrik's 'globalisation trilemma', which combination cannot be achieved simultaneously?
options: Deep economic integration, democratic politics and national sovereignty
A fixed exchange rate, free capital movement and an independent monetary policy
Free trade and capital controls
Economic growth, equality and environmental sustainability
questions.why: Rodrik argues countries can have at most two of hyperglobalisation, democracy and national sovereignty. The exchange-rate option is the separate Mundell–Fleming 'impossible trinity'.

questions.q: What does Ruggie mean by 'embedded liberalism', and why do some argue it was eroded after the 1980s?
markScheme: Post-1945 compromise: multilateral trade liberalisation combined with domestic intervention and welfare
Bretton Woods permitted capital controls and safeguards so markets served social purposes
Erosion: capital account liberalisation, Washington Consensus, deeper WTO integration (Rodrik's hyperglobalisation)
Consequence: loss of protection for workers, contributing to backlash
questions.modelAnswer: Ruggie (1982) used 'embedded liberalism' to describe the post-1945 Bretton Woods compromise: states committed to multilateral trade liberalisation, but within a framework that allowed capital controls, safeguards and domestic intervention to secure full employment and welfare. Liberal markets were embedded in social purposes. From the 1980s, critics argue, the balance eroded as capital controls were dismantled, the Washington Consensus spread market reforms and the WTO pushed integration deeper into domestic regulation, producing what Rodrik calls hyperglobalisation. The perceived loss of protection for workers helps explain later populist backlash.

questions.q: 'Globalisation has made the state obsolete.' Discuss this claim. In your answer, compare the hyperglobalist, sceptical and transformationalist positions, and use evidence from at least two major events since 2008 to assess whether states have lost, retained or reconfigured their power.
markScheme: Defines globalisation (Held et al.) and states the hyperglobalist thesis (Ohmae)
Evidence for erosion: capital mobility, MNC power, constraints on fiscal and monetary autonomy; Strange's retreat of the state
Sceptical response: Hirst and Thompson on regionalised trade, pre-1914 openness and continuing state capacity
Transformationalist view: power reconfigured and sovereignty pooled (e.g. the EU), not ended
Evidence of state resurgence: 2008 bank bailouts, COVID-19 border closures and fiscal support, tariffs (2018, 2025), sanctions on Russia (2022)
States as authors of globalisation (Bretton Woods, WTO), not merely its victims
Uneven effects: strong versus weak states; IMF conditionality
Justified conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
Held and colleagues define globalisation as the widening, deepening and speeding up of worldwide interconnectedness. Hyperglobalists such as Ohmae drew a radical conclusion: in a borderless economy, mobile capital and multinational firms would make the nation-state an unnatural, even obsolete, unit. Susan Strange's The Retreat of the State argued in a similar spirit that authority was migrating from states to markets.

There is real evidence of constraint. Capital can exit countries whose taxes or regulations it dislikes, multinational firms organise production across borders, and financial markets punish governments seen as fiscally irresponsible. Smaller and poorer states, especially those dependent on IMF lending, have found their policy options narrowed by conditionality.

Yet sceptics such as Hirst and Thompson argued that the world economy is international rather than global, concentrated among rich regions, and that pre-1914 openness was comparable. Above all, events since 2008 contradict obsolescence. In the financial crisis, only states could rescue banking systems, through bailouts and central bank intervention. During COVID-19, governments closed borders, restricted movement and financed huge support schemes, demonstrating formidable capacity. The US imposed sweeping tariffs in 2018 and again in 2025, and Western states deployed financial sanctions against Russia after 2022 by exploiting their control of key financial networks. These are states reshaping globalisation, not being dissolved by it.

The transformationalist position fits best. States created the institutions of globalisation, from Bretton Woods to the WTO, and they remain central, but their power is reconfigured: sovereignty is pooled in bodies like the EU, and governance is shared with private and international actors. The effects are uneven: powerful states can use interdependence as a weapon, while weak states experience it as constraint.

The claim is therefore false. Globalisation has changed the context in which states operate and reduced the autonomy of some, but the state remains the indispensable actor in managing, and increasingly contesting, global integration.

questions.q: Tamsa, a fictional middle-income democracy, joined the WTO 25 years ago and opened its capital account. Trade has risen from 30 per cent to 75 per cent of GDP and real GDP per capita has doubled, with population roughly constant. Yet manufacturing employment in its northern region has fallen by 35 per cent, and the top 1 per cent's share of national income has risen from 8 to 15 per cent. A newly elected government proposes 25 per cent tariffs on manufactured imports from its largest trading partner and controls on short-term capital flows. Foreign investors threaten to relocate, and the partner hints it could restrict exports of a critical mineral on which Tamsa's electronics sector depends. (a) Calculate the growth in real average income of the top 1 per cent and of the remaining 99 per cent over the period. (b) Use Rodrik's trilemma and Ruggie's embedded liberalism to analyse the government's dilemma. (c) Explain the partner's threat using the concept of weaponised interdependence. (d) Evaluate the proposed measures from liberal, realist and Marxist perspectives and recommend a course of action.
markScheme: Top 1 per cent: share of income rises from 0.08Y to 0.15 × 2Y = 0.30Y, a 3.75-fold increase (+275 per cent)
Remaining 99 per cent: from 0.92Y to 0.85 × 2Y = 1.70Y, about 1.85-fold (+85 per cent); gains real but unequal, and national averages conceal regional losers
Rodrik's trilemma: hyperglobalisation, democracy and national sovereignty cannot all be held; Tamsa's democratic choice clashes with deep integration
Embedded liberalism: earlier compromise permitted capital controls and safeguards; the proposals as an attempt to re-embed markets
Links to China-shock evidence (Autor, Dorn and Hanson) and Milanovic's elephant curve
Weaponised interdependence: partner exploits a chokepoint in a network; real analogues such as China's export controls on gallium and germanium (2023) and rare earths (2025)
Liberal evaluation: tariffs reduce efficiency, invite retaliation and may breach WTO commitments; prefer adjustment assistance
Realist evaluation: relative gains and supply-chain security; diversification and friend-shoring
Marxist evaluation: capital mobility as structural power disciplining democracy; class distribution of gains
Notes the weakened WTO dispute system (Appellate Body paralysed since 2019 and still blocked after MC14 in 2026) affects enforcement and retaliation
Reasoned, feasible recommendation acknowledging trade-offs
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) With population constant, total income Y doubles to 2Y. The top 1 per cent received 0.08Y and now receive 0.15 × 2Y = 0.30Y, a 3.75-fold rise (275 per cent). The remaining 99 per cent received 0.92Y and now receive 0.85 × 2Y = 1.70Y, about 1.85 times as much (85 per cent). Most people are better off on average, but the gains are skewed to the top, and averages conceal a northern region that has lost over a third of its manufacturing jobs.

(b) Rodrik's trilemma holds that a country cannot simultaneously pursue hyperglobalisation, democratic politics and national sovereignty. Tamsa's voters have used democracy to demand protection, which collides with the deep integration and open capital account it adopted. Ruggie's embedded liberalism shows this is not unprecedented: the Bretton Woods order allowed capital controls and safeguards so that open trade did not override domestic social goals. The government is in effect trying to re-embed markets. The pattern resembles the China shock documented by Autor, Dorn and Hanson and the lower-middle stagnation captured in Milanovic's elephant curve.

(c) The partner's threat illustrates weaponised interdependence (Farrell and Newman). Where a state controls a chokepoint in a global network, it can cut others off to coerce them. China's export controls on gallium and germanium from 2023 and on rare earths in 2025 are real examples of states using control of critical inputs as leverage.

(d) Liberals would oppose the tariffs: they raise consumer and input costs, invite retaliation, may breach WTO commitments and protect declining sectors rather than helping workers adjust; they would favour retraining, regional investment and redistribution through taxation. Realists would see the mineral threat as proof that dependence on a single partner is a security vulnerability and would prioritise diversification, stockpiles and supply chains with allies, valuing resilience over efficiency. Marxists would read investors' threats to relocate as the structural power of capital disciplining a democratic government, and the income data as evidence that globalisation's gains flow to capital. Enforcement is complicated because the WTO's Appellate Body has been unable to hear appeals since 2019, and the 2026 ministerial conference (MC14) did not fix this.

I would recommend targeted rather than blanket measures: temporary safeguards for the most affected sectors, a substantial adjustment and regional development programme, prudential controls on short-term capital flows (which the IMF now accepts in some circumstances), and urgent diversification of critical mineral supplies. This re-embeds integration without inviting a damaging trade war.

questions.q: What key design feature distinguishes the Paris Agreement (2015) from the Kyoto Protocol (1997)?
options: Paris imposes legally binding emission targets on developed countries only
Paris relies on nationally determined contributions from all parties, reviewed through a transparency framework and five-yearly global stocktakes
Paris exempts developing countries from any commitments
Paris authorises binding trade sanctions against non-compliant parties
questions.why: Paris is bottom-up and universal, with self-determined pledges and procedural obligations; Kyoto set top-down binding targets for developed countries only.

questions.q: Explain why climate change is often described as a collective action problem.
markScheme: A stable climate is a global public good: non-excludable and non-rival
Each state bears the full cost of its own cuts but receives only a small, diffuse and delayed share of the benefits, creating incentives to free-ride
If all reason this way, mitigation is under-provided and all are worse off (Hardin's tragedy of the commons)
questions.modelAnswer: A stable climate is a global public good: no state can be excluded from its benefits, and one state's enjoyment does not reduce another's. Each state bears the full cost of its own emissions cuts but receives only a small share of the benefits, which are spread across the world and into the future, so each has an incentive to free-ride on others' efforts. If all reason this way, emissions reductions are under-provided and everyone ends up worse off, the logic of Hardin's tragedy of the commons.

questions.q: Why did the Montreal Protocol succeed where climate agreements have struggled? Evaluate, using at least two IR theories.
markScheme: Structural differences: few producers of ozone-depleting substances and affordable substitutes (e.g. DuPont's alternatives)
Clear, vivid science (the Antarctic ozone hole reported in 1985); constructivist role of an epistemic community (Haas)
Liberal institutionalist design: Multilateral Fund, trade restrictions on non-parties, adjustment procedures
Climate difficulty: fossil fuels embedded across economies, many emitters, contested distribution of costs (CBDR)
Realist point: US–China rivalry raises relative-gains concerns
Evaluative judgement, e.g. institutions work best when interests are already partly aligned; Kigali shows Montreal also aids climate
